title: Khalsa College, 1892
hookLine: a Sikh college rises in Amritsar

cards: Outside Amritsar, on open ground along the road toward Lahore, a crowd gathers for a foundation stone. British officials in formal dress. Supporters from the Sikh princely states.
Singh Sabha reformers, teachers and writers. And ordinary Sikhs who've given what they could, so that this could happen.
Nothing stands there yet but a stone and a plan: a college where young Sikhs can learn science and English without being taught to leave their Gurus behind.

teach.b: First, why a college. The Singh Sabha reformers had schools and papers.
But young Sikhs who wanted higher study went to colleges run by the government or by missions, and some, as the reformers saw it, came back strangers to their own tradition.
The reformers wanted a place that taught the modern subjects and Sikh learning under one roof. Second, who paid. Sikh rulers of the princely states gave large sums.

The British government gave its support. And collections went around the Punjab, in towns and villages, from people with little to spare. The college belonged, in that sense, to everyone who put something in.
Third, the name. Khalsa is the name Guru Gobind Singh gave the community of the initiated, those who belong directly to the Guru.

A Khalsa College says what it's for: a college for that community, open to learning from anywhere, rooted in the Guru's word. Over time, a great building rose on that ground, and generations of students passed through it.
Fourth, what the Gurus say about learning.
In a hymn in Asa, Guru Nanak says that when learning is truly reflected on, the learned one becomes a help to others. Learning that stays in the head, or serves only pride, misses the point.
The founders hoped the college would turn out graduates who served: teachers, doctors, writers and leaders who carried what they'd learned back into the Panth.

how: Sikhs remember Khalsa College in Amritsar as a fruit of the Singh Sabha reform, built with gifts from Sikh princes and ordinary Sikhs, and it still teaches students today.

games.q: young Sikhs want higher study, and some come back strangers to their tradition. what do the reformers do?
o: found a college that teaches modern subjects and Sikh learning together.
games.why: they founded Khalsa College in Amritsar, funded by princes, officials and ordinary Sikhs.

practice: Choose one small thing you'd like to learn, a word of Punjabi, a line of a hymn, how a plant grows, the name of a street you walk down, and hold it as a question: breathe in curious, breathe out patient.
Then ask who it could help once you know it, and let that person come to mind. If you pray, rest in Waheguru as the question settles.

wordCard.voice: Khalsa College. The Sikh college founded in Amritsar to teach modern subjects alongside the Gurus' learning, built with gifts from princes and ordinary Sikhs. Today's word.

orig.note: Khalsa, the community of the initiated, the Guru's own.

carryVoice: Your line: a college for the khalsa. A college is a promise that learning will be passed on. Back tomorrow.
